demonstration.caption: At 0.8c, if Earth measures 10 seconds, how much proper time passes on the ship?

history.text: Imagine the ship travels very fast. Will its clock tick the same amount as the clock on Earth?
In Earth’s frame, the ship travels at 0.80 times light speed. Compare a 10 second Earth interval with 6.00 seconds of ship proper time. We assume constant velocity, with no turnaround.
We have advanced the actual model by 10 Earth seconds. The ship clock reads 6.00 seconds. Gamma is 1.6667, so ship proper time equals Earth time divided by gamma.
At 0.8c, if Earth measures 10 seconds, how much proper time passes on the ship?

correction.caption: Let’s compare your prediction with the measured result. In Earth’s frame, gamma is 1.6667. Ten divided by gamma is 6 seconds, not ten. The ship’s proper time is measured along its own path. This is not an absolute ranking of whose clock is slow.

frame.caption: Neither clock is broken. For two inertial observers, each can describe the other’s moving clock as ticking more slowly; they compare different sets of simultaneous events. The selected journey interval is defined in the Earth frame. Switching the frame changes coordinates, not the ship’s accumulated proper time for those same events. Reuniting the clocks requires a turnaround, which this model does not include.

Why does the moving clock tick slower?

[Prepared answer · offline] In the Earth frame, light in a moving light-clock takes a longer diagonal path between its mirrors. Light’s speed is still c, so more Earth time passes between ticks. At 0.990c, γ is 7.089: an Earth interval of 20.00 seconds corresponds to 2.82 seconds aboard. The ship observer does not feel their own time slowing.
